name: Caroline, Commonwealth, and Restoration Period
description: The literature of Britain from the accession of Charles I through the Civil Wars and Interregnum to the Restoration and the close of the seventeenth century. It spans three distinct political cultures: the Caroline court (1625–1642), whose masque-loving ceremonialism nourished the Cavalier poets and the last flourishing of the private theatres; the Commonwealth and Protectorate (1642–1660), in which the theatres were closed, Puritan and radical sectarian prose proliferated, and Milton produced his polemics and, after the Restoration, Paradise Lost; and the Restoration (1660–1700), which reopened the theatres (now admitting women players), gave birth to the comedy of manners, heroic drama, and modern verse satire, and saw the rise of the Royal Society, the new empirical philosophy of Hobbes and Locke, the prose of Browne, Walton, Pepys, and Bunyan, and the first professional women writers, Behn and Cavendish. The period is the crucible of modern English prose and of a self-consciously 'Augustan' poetics that Dryden codified and that the eighteenth century inherited.
